# `modelTest()` {#fn-modeltest}

In S02, identical candidate bearings produced identical directly constructed observed and simulated densities on build 2.0.9008. Global rejection at the 5 percent level ranged from 4.35 to 5.50 percent under the six matched null designs. [S02 results](s02-specified-models.qmd).

**Verified on 2.0.9006.** The observed and simulated azimuth curves use the same circular cluster search. The original test matrix gave one interval from 346° to 15°. [S03 rerun](s03-scoring-checks.qmd).

**Validation on 2.0.9005.** Independent scoring reproduced the stored linear-grid probabilities. A north-crossing azimuth excess can split into two clusters; including both 0 and 360 degrees can also affect the global rank. [S03 results](s03-scoring-checks.qmd).

A directly measured triangular density follows the sampled mode, retaining its left/right proportions. Both softened uniform families preserve their second width in degrees. [Measurement families](orientation-densities.qmd#measurement-families).

[Function index](function-index.html#idx-modeltest)

```{=html}
<p>A proposed topographical or astronomical explanation can predict some orientations more
frequently than others. Testing that explanation requires simulating its predicted
distribution at the sites under study.
</p>
<p>Silva and Lomsdalen (2025) extended the random-orientation framework of Silva (2020)
to test specific hypotheses about temple orientations in Malta, including topographical and
astronomical explanations. Here the hypothesis specifies the relative probability of each
candidate orientation. A small global p-value is evidence against that particular model.
</p>
```

**Model weights and interpretation.**

```{=html}
<p>Weights are discrete sampling probabilities up to proportionality. If a
continuous model is evaluated on an uneven coordinate grid, density heights
alone do not represent probability mass; construct weights that account for
the bin widths before calling the function. Put site-specific model tables in
the same order as the observed measurements.
</p>
<p>A large p-value does not prove the proposed explanation or measure its
probability. The test asks whether the specified model is incompatible with
the observed departure statistic. Alternative models can remain compatible.
The simulations do not automatically represent dependence between sites,
selection after viewing the data, or uncertainty in fitted model parameters.
See <code>randomTest</code> for study-design and Monte Carlo limitations.
</p>



```

**Interpretation and limits.** Preserve the generating model, measurement-to-site mapping, simulation seed, comparison grid and rank convention. A change in the null answers a different archaeological question even when the same observed curve is used.

<table><thead><tr><th>Argument</th><th>Formal default</th><th>Behaviour in this interface</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row"><code>pdf</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Empirical skyscapeR.pdf from <code>az.pdf</code>, <code>dec.pdf</code> or <code>coordtrans</code>. Omit to reuse stored measurement uncertainties or mean-shift transformed declination curves.
